_note: WHY A FIELD IS NOT READ. Every audit run reports the same NOT-FOUND list until somebody says what they decided about each name, and re-judging 186 names on every run is how a real finding gets lost in a list nobody finishes reading. A key recorded here is still counted, still shown as DECIDED, and drops out of the NEW column -- so NEW means what it says: this upstream is sending something nobody has looked at yet.
_key_format: <host>::<field>, or *::<field> to apply the decision to every upstream. Host is the first segment of the capture filename, which capture_upstreams.py writes host-first.

_verdicts.declined: seen, judged, deliberately not wired. `why` must say what question it would answer and why that question is not worth a field.
_verdicts.envelope: protocol scaffolding rather than data -- a wrapper, an echo of our own request, or a transport detail. Reading it would not add a fact.
_verdicts.wired-elsewhere: the fact IS used, reached by a different name or from a different source. `why` must name that source.

waterservices.usgs.gov::queryInfo.why: WaterML wraps every response in an echo of the request. queryURL, locationParam, variableParam and criteria are the URL this app just built.

waterservices.usgs.gov::queryURL.why: our own request, read back to us.

waterservices.usgs.gov::locationParam.why: our own request, read back to us.

waterservices.usgs.gov::variableParam.why: our own request, read back to us.

waterservices.usgs.gov::declaredType.why: the Java class name of the response type. Not a fact about water.

waterservices.usgs.gov::sourceInfo.why: the container holding site name and coordinates. This app already knows both -- the binding put the site there.

waterservices.usgs.gov::siteCode.why: the site number is the argument fetchUsgs was called with.

waterservices.usgs.gov::agencyCode.why: always USGS on a USGS endpoint.

waterservices.usgs.gov::geoLocation.why: the gauge's coordinates come from water_bindings.json, which is also what decided this gauge belongs to this water.

waterservices.usgs.gov::localSiteXY.why: state-plane coordinates. This app is in WGS84 everywhere.

waterservices.usgs.gov::siteProperty.why: county code, state code, HUC and site type. The binder already holds all four per gauge and they do not change between refreshes.

waterservices.usgs.gov::timeZoneInfo.why: the container for the two zone blocks below.

waterservices.usgs.gov::defaultTimeZone.why: dateTime on every point carries its own offset. A separate zone table is a second way to get the same answer wrong.

waterservices.usgs.gov::variableID.why: USGS's internal row id for the parameter. parameterCd is the identifier this app and every other consumer uses.

waterservices.usgs.gov::variableName.why: 'Streamflow, ft³/s' -- HTML-entity encoded and unit-suffixed. This app labels its own readings and would have to strip the entity to use it.

waterservices.usgs.gov::variableProperty.why: empty container on every series in the capture.

waterservices.usgs.gov::unitCode.why: the unit is fixed per parameter code -- 00010 is degC, 00060 is ft3/s, 00062 is ft -- and the mapping in fetchUsgs is written against those. A per-response unit would only matter if USGS started serving a code in two units, which would break the mapping loudly rather than silently.

waterservices.usgs.gov::valueType.why: 'Derived Value' vs 'Measured Value'. Discharge is always derived from stage through a rating curve; saying so on screen would not change a decision about where to fish.

waterservices.usgs.gov::optionCode.why: the statistic option, always 00000 on instantaneous values.

waterservices.usgs.gov::noDataValue.why: the sentinel is -999999 on every series and fetchUsgs rejects it numerically. Reading it per-series would replace a constant with a fetch.

waterservices.usgs.gov::qualifierCode.why: 'P' provisional vs 'A' approved. Essentially every instantaneous reading is provisional -- approval runs a year or more behind -- so a provisional badge would sit on every number this app shows and mean nothing. The qualifiers that DO matter (Ice, Eqp, Mnt) arrive as the -999999 sentinel, which is already rejected.

waterservices.usgs.gov::qualityControlLe.why: empty on every series in the capture; the same fact as qualifierCode when it is not.

waterservices.usgs.gov::methodID.why: the sensor is chosen by methodDescription, which says TOP or BOTTOM in words. The numeric id says nothing without a lookup.

waterservices.usgs.gov::censorCode.why: below-detection-limit marking. Empty on continuous series; it belongs to discrete lab samples.

api.water.noaa.gov::TruncateObs.why: how many observations the NWPS hydrograph page trims for display. A rendering hint for their chart, not ours.

api.water.noaa.gov::ObservedFloodCategor.why: duplicate of status.observed.floodCategory, which conditions.js reads into flood_category.

api.water.noaa.gov::ForecastFloodCategor.why: duplicate of status.forecast.floodCategory. The forecast block is dropped entirely when primary is the -999 sentinel, which is what this field reports as 'fcst_not_current'.

api.water.noaa.gov::olddatum.why: a per-crest flag saying the historic stage was recorded against a superseded datum. Only reachable through flood.crests, which is itself declined.

api.water.noaa.gov::secondaryUnits.why: the ENVELOPE-level unit label. conditions.js reads status.observed.secondaryUnit instead, on purpose and with the gauges listed: the two disagree, and trusting the envelope turned 4,000 cfs into '4 ft3/s' on the Congaree.

api.water.noaa.gov::generatedTime.why: when NWPS built the response, repeated on all 2,861 points. The observation's own validTime is the time that matters.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::Speci.why: a row-level 'when the message block was last touched'. Every message in SpecialMessage[] carries its own EventDate, which pickNewestMessage already sorts on; on Lake Wateree this row field is 2026-05-01, the OLDER of its two notices. The coarser date would undo the fix.
null on all 34 lakes in the capture. See SpecialMessageUpdated.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::SortO.why: the order Duke's own lake list renders in. This app orders by distance from the person.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::Locat.why: Duke's internal parent-location id. No endpoint takes it; lakepondLocationId is the key /lakes/operating-range wants and that one is read.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::locat.why: see LocationParentId -- the alerts feed spells it lower-case.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::river.why: internal id with no endpoint behind it. riverbasinId is the one that identifies the basin and it is read.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::lakep.why: -1 on the system-wide row and unused elsewhere; lakepondLocationId is the usable key.
the operating-range response echoing the id we passed in the URL.

api.hydro-derived.duke-energy.app::river.why: the long form of the group's riverName ('Catawba - Wateree' vs 'Catawba'). parseAccessAlerts carries riverName into basin_name, which nothing renders -- alerts display place or water. Reading the longer label would not change a screen.

api.water.noaa.gov::secondaryName.why: the stageflow envelope's label for the secondary series. conditions.js reads status.observed.secondaryUnit instead, deliberately: the envelope and the observation disagree, and trusting the envelope turned 4,000 cfs into '4 ft3/s' on the Congaree.

api.water.noaa.gov::issuedTime.why: when NWPS issued the stageflow product. Each observation carries its own time and that is the one the card shows.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::approval_status.why: 'Approved' vs 'Provisional'. Approval runs a year or more behind, so a provisional badge would sit on essentially every live reading and mean nothing. Same call as NWIS qualifierCode.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::unit_of_measure.why: fixed per parameter code, and the only OGC caller (js/modules/usgs-gauges.js) queries parameter_code=00060 explicitly, so the unit cannot vary underneath it.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::time_series_id.why: an opaque hash identifying one series. latest-continuous returns one row per series and the caller filters to a single parameter at a single site; there is nothing to disambiguate with it.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::numberReturned.why: the page size of the response we just asked for.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::storageCrs.why: the collection's declared CRS. Everything here is WGS84 and a mismatch would misplace every point loudly.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::itemType.why: OGC API boilerplate, 'feature' on every collection.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::temporal.why: the collection's overall time extent, null in the capture. The per-series begin/end is the useful form and it is a different endpoint.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::openapi.why: a link to the NIMS API's own schema document.

api.waterdata.usgs.gov::email.why: the NIMS support mailbox, published in their service index.

api.open-meteo.com::generationtime_ms.why: how long Open-Meteo took to build the response.

api.open-meteo.com::utc_offset_seconds.why: the request asks for a fixed timezone and every timestamp comes back in it. A second representation of the same offset is a second chance to be wrong.

api.open-meteo.com::daily_units.why: the units block echoes what the request asked for -- fahrenheit, mph, inch -- and those are pinned in the URL this app builds.

aa.usno.navy.mil::day_of_week.why: derivable from the date this app supplied in the request.

aa.usno.navy.mil::isdst.why: the tz offset is passed in the request; a daylight-saving flag alongside it is a second source for one fact.

forecast.weather.gov::operationalMode.why: 'Production' vs a test instance of the NWS point-forecast service.

forecast.weather.gov::srsName.why: 'WGS 1984', which is the only CRS this app uses.

forecast.weather.gov::creationDate.why: when the NWS product was generated. Each forecast period carries its own valid time and that is what the card shows.

forecast.weather.gov::productionCenter.why: 'Charleston, SC'. The WFO identifier is already read from this same response and is the precise form of the same fact.

forecast.weather.gov::layoutKey.why: the DWML time-layout key that binds periods to times. This app reads the already-flattened JSON arrays.

cwms-data.usace.army.mil::interval-offse.why: minutes past the interval that a series is stamped at. Every value carries its own timestamp.

cwms-data.usace.army.mil::last-update.why: when the CATALOGUE row was last touched, which is not when the series last reported. The data endpoint answers that.

www.tva.com::DamType.why: 'Non-hydropower' vs hydro. TVA publishes generation and release data only for the hydro projects, and a project with no data is already absent from the result.

www.tva.com::AltAbbr1.why: TVA's alternate short code ('Bark' for Barkley). The binder joins on the NWS handbook-5 lid, which is the code every other feed here uses.

www.waterqualitydata.us::OrganizationIde.why: the code beside OrganizationFormalName, which IS read as the programme fallback. A code and its name are one fact.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityIdentif.why: activity bookkeeping on a discrete sample. The fields that place a measurement in the water -- CharacteristicName, ResultMeasureValue, the depth pair, ActivityStartDate -- are all read; these identify the visit, not the water.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityTypeCod.why: activity bookkeeping on a discrete sample. The fields that place a measurement in the water -- CharacteristicName, ResultMeasureValue, the depth pair, ActivityStartDate -- are all read; these identify the visit, not the water.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityComment.why: activity bookkeeping on a discrete sample. The fields that place a measurement in the water -- CharacteristicName, ResultMeasureValue, the depth pair, ActivityStartDate -- are all read; these identify the visit, not the water.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityStartTi.why: the clock time of a grab sample. WQP records are summarised by DATE and by month; a lake's July temperature does not turn on whether the boat went out at 9 or at 11.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityEndDate.why: a grab sample starts and ends in the same minute; the end fields are empty or equal to the start on continuous-profile rows too.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityDepthAl.why: which surface the depth is measured from. Every WQP depth this app uses is below the water surface, and a row that meant something else would be an outlier the depth clamp already rejects.

www.waterqualitydata.us::SampleAquifer.why: groundwater bookkeeping. This app reads lakes and rivers.

www.waterqualitydata.us::HydrologicCondi.why: 'stable, low stage' and similar, filled by some agencies and not others. USGS gauge readings answer stage for the same water, continuously and for every day rather than for sample days.

www.waterqualitydata.us::SampleCollectio.why: a discrete lab sample's paperwork. limnology.js summarises WQP as measurements by characteristic, depth and date; who ran the analysis and on what instrument does not change a temperature profile or a secchi reading.

www.waterqualitydata.us::DetectionQuanti.why: detection limits matter for contaminants near zero. Temperature, dissolved oxygen, secchi depth and turbidity are never near a detection limit.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultDetection.why: 'Not Detected' and similar, and those rows arrive with an empty ResultMeasureValue, which parseFloat already drops.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultSampleFra.why: 'Total' vs 'Dissolved'. Meaningful for metals and nutrients; the five characteristics this app requests have no fractions.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultStatusIde.why: 'Final' vs 'Preliminary'. Same call as NWIS qualifierCode -- it would sit on nearly every row.

www.waterqualitydata.us::StatisticalBase.why: empty on grab samples; it labels pre-aggregated rows, which this app does not request.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultValueType.why: 'Actual' vs 'Estimated'. An estimated secchi reading is still the only secchi reading that lake has.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultWeightBas.why: wet vs dry weight, for tissue and sediment results. Not applicable to water measurements.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultTimeBasis.why: the averaging period for a computed result. Grab samples have none.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultTemperatu.why: the temperature a lab result was normalised to. Applies to chemistry, not to the water temperature itself.

www.waterqualitydata.us::PrecisionValue.why: the analytical precision of a lab result. See DetectionQuantitationLimitTypeName.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ResultCommentTe.why: free text from the sampling agency, mostly empty and never in a fixed vocabulary.

www.waterqualitydata.us::MeasureQualifie.why: lab qualifier flags. The ones that matter arrive as an empty ResultMeasureValue, which is already dropped.

www.waterqualitydata.us::USGSPCode.why: the NWIS parameter code for a WQP row. This app selects WQP rows by CharacteristicName, which is the vocabulary WQP itself is keyed on and the only one STORET providers populate.

www.waterqualitydata.us::SubjectTaxonomi.why: fish and invertebrate tissue sampling. Not a water measurement.

waterservices.usgs.gov::agency_cd.why: always USGS on these requests, and the binder joins on the site number alone.

waterservices.usgs.gov::coord_acy_cd.why: how precisely the site's coordinates are known. The binder's name+geometry test already refuses a match that is not inside the water.

waterservices.usgs.gov::dec_coord_datum_.why: NAD83 on every row in all four state catalogues.

waterservices.usgs.gov::alt_va.why: the GAUGE's land-surface altitude, not the water's. Pool elevation comes from the reading, not from where the instrument sits.

waterservices.usgs.gov::huc_cd.why: the hydrologic unit. The binder decides which water a gauge belongs to by name AND geometry against the actual shoreline, which is a stronger test than sharing a HUC.

waterservices.usgs.gov::parm_grp_cd.why: USGS's parameter grouping. This app selects by parameter code.

waterservices.usgs.gov::access_cd.why: public vs restricted access to the series. A restricted series simply returns nothing.

waterservices.usgs.gov::tz_cd.why: the RDB timezone column. Each row's datetime is read together with it in the fallback path and the JSON path carries offsets inline.

waterservices.usgs.gov::value_qualifier_.why: the RDB spelling of qualifierCode -- 'P' provisional on essentially every live reading. The qualifiers that matter (Ice, Eqp, Mnt) arrive as the -999999 sentinel, which fetchUsgs rejects numerically.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ActivityTopDept.why: MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. Two real resultPhysChem responses on 2026-08-25 -- Lake Murray (Lexington Co, SC), 3,080 rows, and Hartwell Lake (Anderson Co, SC/GA), 7,872 rows, covering SCDES and Georgia DNR EPD -- carry ZERO non-empty values in the ActivityTop/BottomDepthHeightMeasure pair. Neither agency states depth as an interval. GA EPD uses ResultDepthHeightMeasure (4,340 rows) and limnology.js already falls back to it; SCDES publishes single-depth grab samples, one result per activity, with no profile to attach a depth interval to. A fallback here would have been built on a guess.

www.waterqualitydata.us::ProjectIdentifi.why: read as the FALLBACK for `programs` when a row has no OrganizationFormalName. The organisation wins because it is the answer a person wants: Murray shows 11 project codes against 1 organisation, Hartwell 11 against 2 -- and the 2 are the fact worth showing, since Georgia and South Carolina both monitor that lake.

forecast.weather.gov::metar.why: the id of the ASOS station the observation came from. conditions.js already reads it as `currentobservation.id` into `observation.station` -- 'KNBC', Beaufort MCAS -- alongside the station's own name and coordinates, so the distance from the water can be measured rather than assumed. Two fields, one fact.

forecast.weather.gov::Weatherimage.why: 'bkn.png', the filename of an NWS sky-cover icon. `currentobservation.Weather` carries the same sky state as words -- 'Mostly Cloudy' -- and that IS read, into observation.weather. A remote image URL would be an asset fetched from weather.gov to say what a string already in hand says.

forecast.weather.gov::iconLink.why: the per-period forecast icon URLs. See Weatherimage: the forecast text is already read and an icon is a rendering choice, not a fact about the water.

forecast.weather.gov::hazardUrl.why: a link to the active hazard product. conditions.js queries the NWS WWA service directly at the point -- mapservices.weather.noaa.gov/eventdriven/WWA -- which returns the hazards themselves rather than a page about them, and does it for a point rather than a zone.

forecast.weather.gov::firezone.why: the NWS fire weather zone, 'SCZ149'. It answers a question about burning conditions on land. The marine and public zone ids from this same response ARE read, because they are how the marine forecast and the WWA query are addressed.
